title: Why is Education So Damn Fad-Prone?
author: Robert Pondiscio
summary: Robert Pondiscio asks why education cycles through frameworks such as twenty-first century skills, trauma-informed pedagogy, flipped classrooms and 1:1 devices, and rejects the easy answer that educators are gullible. He argues that classroom teachers are typically the least enthusiastic participants and that the system makes churn rational. Four structural forces explain it: weak feedback loops, leadership legitimacy that requires visible change, low barriers to new ideas, and moral urgency that favors acting over waiting. The real problem, he says, is that schools struggle to sustain success once they find it, since improvement tends to come from unglamorous coherence, teacher expertise and consistent routines. Houston's recent reforms illustrate disciplined execution over novelty. His proposal is to realign incentives so stability and implementation fidelity are valued as forms of leadership and competence is made visible.
points: Education's fad cycle is a feature of the system's incentives, not a failure of educator judgment.
Weak feedback loops make it hard to prove an approach works, leaving the field vulnerable to premature abandonment of good ideas as well as adoption of bad ones.
School leaders signal legitimacy through visible initiatives, and with superintendents lasting about one contract cycle, continuity looks like passivity.
Low barriers let frameworks scale through PD and procurement before effectiveness is established, while moral urgency makes waiting for evidence feel unethical.
The remedy is to reward continuity and implementation fidelity, treating execution as an achievement and making competence visible.
quotes: The easy answer is also the most insulting—that educators are uniquely susceptible to trends, quick to abandon what works, and too eager to embrace whatever comes next.
In education, by contrast, the signal is slow and noisy. Instructional changes may take years to show results. Student cohorts turn over annually. Outcomes depend on factors well beyond the classroom
A leader who says, “We’re going to keep doing what we’re doing, but do it better,” risks appearing passive or directionless, even if the system is performing well. It is a structural expectation.

Professional development cycles spread new ideas quickly, consultants package innovations into turnkey programs, and procurement systems often treat instructional approaches as interchangeable. The result is a highly permeable system—one in which ideas can enter and scale rapidly, often long before their effectiveness is firmly established.

Waiting for perfect evidence can feel ethically unacceptable; trying something new, even with incomplete proof, feels compassionate. This isn’t foolish or irresponsible. It’s what happens when moral responsibility collides with uncertainty. But it creates a powerful bias toward action—and, by extension, toward constant change.

Schools that improve often do so through unglamorous means: adopting a coherent curriculum, building teacher expertise, reinforcing consistent instructional routines, and maintaining focus over time. None of this is flashy.

In short, we need to make competence visible. Because until we do, the system will continue to reward the appearance of change over the reality of improvement. So yes, education is fad-prone. Just not for the reasons we usually assume. We don’t chase reform because we forget what works. We chase reform because the system makes standing still look irresponsible—even when standing still is exactly what success requires.
